new_statements.rule_in_words: The most authoritative accessible source states explicitly that the position of the Middle Mongol accent is not known: the written sources show no reduction of unaccented syllables, so they neither confirm nor refute the conjecture (based on Dagur and central Mongolic) that accent was originally on the first syllable. Secondary/reading-pronunciation sources for Written (Classical) Mongolian put the stress on the first syllable (Poppe 1954 §15, p. 9: 'always falling upon the first syllable regardless of vocalic length'; Grønbech & Krueger 1955 §3: non-phonemic, read on the first syllable), and Atwood's 2023 translator's note says stress on Middle Mongolian names 'is generally on the first syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Middle Mongol in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Middle Mongol. Nugteren notes (p. 76) that the restriction of *o/*ö to first syllables 'may be an indication for initial accent, at least in the period when this distribution of the vowels was established' (i.e. pre-Middle-Mongol), and that modern Dagur/central Mongolic have initial accent while Shirongol/Moghol have final accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Extinct corpus language attested only in scripts (Uighur-Mongolian, 'Phags-pa, Chinese and Arabic transcriptions); no direct evidence of accent placement. The statement concerns word-level accent; Nugteren adds (p. 60) that Common Mongolic accent placement is an undecided matter and 'probably non-distinctive'.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Nugteren 2011) is about Middle Mongol proper (13th-14th c. corpus language, Glottolog midd1351). The positive first-syllable statements found (Poppe 1954 §15; Grønbech & Krueger 1955 §3) describe Written/Classical Mongolian reading pronunciation, which Glottolog files under midd1351 via Janhunen's 'Written Mongol' chapter but which is a different (literary, Uighur-script) variety; Glottolog's midd1351 page lists no alternative names or dialects. Atwood 2023 is a translator's pronunciation guide for Middle Mongolian names, not a description.
